MESSAGE:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.

REQUESTS:
1. Explain what 'lippage' means in tiling
2. Suggest a grout colour for pale grey porcelain tile
3. Say whether to tile before or after fitting the new toilet, with a reason
4. Calculate how many boxes of 30x60 cm tiles (8 per box) are needed for a 2.4 x 1.8 m floor plus 10% waste  KEY: Area = 2.4 x 1.8 = 4.32 m^2; tile = 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18 m^2, so 24 tiles exactly. Plus 10% = 26.4, round up to 27 tiles. 27/8 = 3.375, so 4 boxes (32 tiles). 3 boxes (24 tiles) is the no-waste shortcut and would leave them short. Answer: 4 boxes.
5. Write a short polite message to neighbours about tile-cutting noise
6. Give three tips for a beginner laying a floor

ANSWER:
Not too many questions at all. Here's everything.

## What "lippage" means
Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits higher than the tile next to it, so the floor has a little "lip" you can feel with your foot or see in raking light. It's especially common with long tiles like your 30 × 60s, because they're often very slightly bowed. Two things help:
- a **tile levelling clip system**, which is cheap and very beginner-friendly;
- laying the tiles in a brick pattern offset by **a third** of a tile rather than a half.

## Grout colour
Go for a **mid-grey**, a shade or two darker than the tile. It hides everyday dirt far better than white or very pale grout, and it still looks clean against pale grey porcelain. For even more stain resistance, use a stain-resistant or epoxy grout, or seal a standard cement grout once it's cured.

## Floor or toilet first?
Do the **floor first**. The toilet then sits on finished tiles, you avoid fiddly cuts around its base, and you can replace the toilet later without disturbing the floor.

## How many boxes
- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**.
- Each tile: 0.3 × 0.6 = **0.18 m²**, so you need **24 tiles** exactly.
- Adding 10%: 26.4, round up to **27 tiles**.
- At 8 tiles a box: 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, so **buy 4 boxes** (32 tiles).

Three boxes would give you exactly 24 tiles with nothing to spare for cuts or a cracked tile, so you do need the fourth box. The extra tiles aren't wasted:
- A brick pattern produces more offcuts than the 10% rule assumes, so you may well use some of them.
- Keep any left over in case you ever need to replace a tile.
- Check the boxes all share the same **batch number**, because shades can vary between batches.

## Message to the neighbours
> Hi [names], just a heads-up that I'll be cutting tiles on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise between about [9] and [12]. Sorry for the disruption, and thanks for being so patient about the skip. It should be gone soon! [Your name]

## Three tips for your first floor
1. **Lay the tiles out dry first, without adhesive.** Find the layout that avoids thin slivers at the doorway or along the most visible wall, and mark a straight starting line. Most beginner floors that look "off" go wrong at this stage.
2. **Get the base right.** The floor underneath must be flat, solid, clean and dry. On timber, that usually means plywood or tile backer board screwed down well. Use a flexible adhesive, and spread it on the back of each tile as well as the floor ("back-buttering") so there are no hollow spots.
3. **Work in small sections and check as you go.** Lay a few tiles, then check them with a level and the clips. Wipe adhesive out of the joints before it sets, and wait the full drying time before grouting. Going slowly is the trick the videos don't show you.

You'll be fine. The fact that you're thinking it through this carefully is a good sign.
